In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''level structure''' on a [[space (mathematics)|space]] ''X'' is an extra structure attached to ''X'' that shrinks or eliminates the [[automorphism group]] of ''X'', by demanding automorphisms to preserve the level structure; attaching a level structure is often phrased as '''rigidifying''' the geometry of ''X''.<ref>{{harvnb|Mumford|Fogarty|Kirwan|1994|loc=Ch. 7.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Katz|Mazur|1985|loc=Introduction}}</ref>

In applications, a level structure is used in the construction of [[moduli space]]s; a moduli space is often constructed as a quotient. The presence of automorphisms poses a difficulty to forming a [[quotient (algebraic geometry)|quotient]]; thus introducing level structures helps overcome this difficulty.

There is no single definition of a level structure; rather, depending on the space ''X'', one introduces the notion of a level structure. The classic one is that on an [[elliptic curve]] (see [[#Example: an abelian scheme]]). There is a level structure attached to a [[formal group]] called a '''Drinfeld level structure''', introduced in {{harv|Drinfeld|1974}}.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://publications.ias.edu/sites/default/files/Number59.pdf|title=Survey of Drinfeld's modules|last1=Deligne|first1=P.|author-link1=Pierre Deligne|last2=Husemöller|first2=D.|author-link2=Dale Husemoller|year=1987|journal=Contemp. Math.|volume=67|issue=1|pages=25–91|doi=10.1090/conm/067/902591}}</ref>

== Level structures on elliptic curves ==
Classically, level structures on elliptic curves <math>E = \mathbb{C}/\Lambda</math> are given by a lattice containing the defining lattice of the variety. From the moduli theory of elliptic curves, all such lattices can be described as the lattice <math>\mathbb{Z}\oplus \mathbb{Z}\cdot \tau</math> for <math>\tau \in \mathfrak{h}</math> in the upper-half plane. Then, the lattice generated by <math>1/n, \tau/n</math> gives a lattice which contains all <math>n</math>-torsion points on the elliptic curve denoted <math>E[n]</math>. In fact, given such a lattice is invariant under the <math>\Gamma(n) \subset \text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})</math> action on <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>, where<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
\Gamma(n) &= \text{ker}(\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) \to \text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}/n)) \\
&= \left\{
M \in \text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z}) : M \equiv \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix} \text{ (mod n)}
\right\}
\end{align}</math></blockquote>hence it gives a point in <math>\Gamma(n)\backslash\mathfrak{h}</math><ref>{{Cite book|last=Silverman|first=Joseph H.|author-link=Joseph H. Silverman|title=The arithmetic of elliptic curves|date=2009|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-0-387-09494-6|edition=2nd|location=New York|pages=439–445|oclc=405546184}}</ref> called the moduli space of level N structures of elliptic curves <math>Y(n)</math>, which is a [[modular curve]]. In fact, this moduli space contains slightly more information: the [[Weil pairing]]<blockquote><math>e_n\left(\frac{1}{n}, \frac{\tau}{n}\right) = e^{2\pi i /n}</math></blockquote>gives a point in the <math>n</math>-th roots of unity, hence in <math>\mathbb{Z}/n</math>.

== Example: an abelian scheme ==
Let <math>X \to S</math> be an [[abelian scheme]] whose geometric fibers have dimension ''g''.

Let ''n'' be a positive integer that is prime to the residue field of each ''s'' in ''S''. For ''n'' ≥ 2, a '''level ''n''-structure''' is a set of sections <math>\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_{2g}</math> such that<ref>{{harvnb|Mumford|Fogarty|Kirwan|1994|loc=Definition 7.1.}}</ref>
# for each geometric point <math>s : S \to X</math>, <math>\sigma_{i}(s)</math> form a basis for the group of points of order ''n'' in <math>\overline{X}_s</math>,
# <math>m_n \circ \sigma_i</math> is the identity section, where <math>m_n</math> is the multiplication by ''n''.

See also: [[modular curve#Examples]], [[moduli stack of elliptic curves]].
